title: You Never Touched Them—but Jesus Still Wants to Talk About What Happened in Your Heart
paragraphs: You Never Touched Them—but Jesus Still Wants to Talk About What Happened in Your Heart

You may have kept your hands clean, your messages deleted, your reputation intact, and your secret invisible. But Jesus has never been interested only in what your hands did. He loves you enough to confront what your heart became.
There are sins nobody can screenshot.
No hotel receipt.
No secret child.
No eyewitness.
No confession whispered through tears to a spouse.
No physical affair anyone could uncover.
Nothing happened.
At least, that is what you keep telling yourself.
You never touched them.
You never kissed them.
You never crossed that final physical line.
And maybe because you did not cross it, you have quietly built a courtroom inside your own mind where you are both defendant and judge.
Your verdict?
“I didn’t actually do anything.”
Then Jesus walks into the courtroom.
And suddenly the question changes.
Not:
“Did you touch them?”
But:
“What happened in your heart?”
That question is terrifying.
And strangely beautiful.
Because Jesus Christ does not expose the heart because He enjoys humiliating sinners.
He exposes what is killing us because He came to save sinners.
Maybe it started innocently.
A conversation.
A friendship.
Someone at work who listened a little more carefully than your spouse seemed to.
Someone online whose attention made you feel attractive again.
Someone at church who understood your struggles.
Someone from your past who suddenly appeared in your notifications.
You told yourself there was nothing wrong with talking.
And perhaps, initially, there wasn’t.
But somewhere along the way, something shifted.
You began waiting for their name to appear.
You started dressing with the possibility of seeing them somewhere in the back of your mind.
You replayed conversations after they ended.
You imagined conversations that had never happened.
You wondered what life might feel like with them.
You compared their tenderness with your spouse’s weaknesses.
Or, if you were single, you allowed desire to turn another human being into the private theater of your imagination.
Nobody knew.
You smiled normally.
You worshiped normally.
You went home normally.
You may even have prayed normally.
But there was another room inside you.
A room you would have been horrified for anyone else to enter.
And this is exactly where the words of Jesus become painfully relevant.
Jesus said:
“Everyone who looks at a woman with lustful intent has already committed adultery with her in his heart.”
Matthew 5:28.
The Greek is devastatingly precise:
πᾶς ὁ βλέπων γυναῖκα πρὸς τὸ ἐπιθυμῆσαι αὐτὴν
pas ho blepōn gynaika pros to epithymēsai autēn
The crucial expression is πρὸς τὸ ἐπιθυμῆσαι—pros to epithymēsai—looking in such a way as to desire, covet, or lust after.
Jesus is not declaring that noticing another person's beauty is automatically adultery.
He is going deeper.
He is confronting the cultivated gaze.
The entertained desire.
The inward consent.
The heart that does not merely experience temptation but begins feeding it.
Then comes the phrase we desperately wish Jesus had omitted:
ἐν τῇ καρδίᾳ αὐτοῦ
en tē kardia autou.
“In his heart.”
There.
That is the room.
That is where Jesus is standing.
And perhaps you immediately feel defensive.
“But I never touched them.”
Jesus knows.
“But I never slept with them.”
Jesus knows.
“I never even told them how I felt.”
Jesus knows that too.
But He also knows what you imagined when nobody was watching.
He knows which conversations you replayed.
He knows whether you secretly wanted their marriage to fail.
He knows whether you compared your spouse to them.
He knows what you searched.
He knows why you returned to that profile.
He knows what you hoped would happen.
He knows the difference between temptation arriving at your door and you quietly pulling out a chair for it.
And before shame convinces you to stop reading, you need to understand something enormously important.
Jesus did not preach Matthew 5 so that respectable sinners could learn to hate themselves more efficiently.
He was demolishing our obsession with external righteousness.
Earlier in the same sermon, He warned that unless our righteousness exceeded that of the scribes and Pharisees, we would not enter the kingdom of heaven.
Then He began pressing beyond behavior into the heart.
Murder?
Look at anger.
Adultery?
Look at lust.
Religious performance?
Look at motive.
Jesus keeps taking the human finger pointing outward and turning it toward the human heart.
Why?
Because the deepest human problem cannot be solved merely by keeping our bodies away from certain locations.
We need new hearts.
That is why this hurts.
Some of us have spent years congratulating ourselves for sins we almost committed physically while secretly nourishing them emotionally.
You remained faithful with your body while becoming unfaithful in fantasy.
You never climbed into their bed.
But you built an imaginary life with them.
You never said, “I love you.”
But you desperately wanted them to say it.
You never removed your wedding ring.
But somewhere inside your imagination, you temporarily removed your covenant.
Perhaps your struggle is pornography.
Perhaps it is someone you know.
Perhaps it is an ex.
Perhaps it is a celebrity.
Perhaps it is the person whose profile you keep checking and would be embarrassed to explain why.
Perhaps there is no particular person at all—only an imagination you have trained to consume bodies without ever considering souls.
And maybe your secret defense has always been:
“At least I haven't actually cheated.”
But Christianity is not ultimately about becoming skillful enough to remain technically innocent.
Jesus wants truth in the inward person.
And here is where the story could become another piece of religious shame.
It could leave you exposed, frightened, and disgusted with yourself.
But that would stop before reaching the Gospel.
Because the same Jesus who exposes lust is the Jesus who receives sinners.
The same Christ who refuses to rename darkness also refuses to abandon the repentant person trapped inside it.
He does not say sin is harmless.
He does something infinitely better.
He bears its judgment.
At the cross, Jesus was not crucified merely for the sins that became visible.
He died for sinners.
For what was done with hands.
For what was spoken with mouths.
For what was entertained in hearts.
For secret rebellion.
For respectable rebellion.
For the darkness everybody discovered.
And the darkness nobody ever did.
Scripture says:
πάντες γὰρ ἥμαρτον
pantes gar hēmarton.
“For all have sinned.”
Romans 3:23.
All.
The adulterer.
The fantasizer.
The pornography addict.
The religious hypocrite.
The lonely spouse who allowed emotional hunger to become secret idolatry.
The single believer who repeatedly feeds lust and then promises God, “This was the last time.”
The pastor.
The teenager.
The husband.
The wife.
The person reading this while thinking, “Nobody knows.”
All have sinned.
But Romans does not end there.
The astonishing announcement of Christianity is not that sinful people can clean themselves sufficiently for God to tolerate them.
The announcement is Jesus Christ.
Romans 5:8 says that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.
Not after we became impressive.
Not after our search history became clean enough.
Not after temptation disappeared.
Not after we repaired our reputation.
Christ moved toward sinners while they were sinners.
That does not make repentance unnecessary.
It makes repentance possible without despair.
Repentance is not pretending you were never dirty.
Repentance is finally agreeing with God about the dirt and running toward the One who can wash you.
The New Testament word often translated “repent” is μετανοεῖτε—metanoeite—a call to turn, to change one's mind and direction in response to God's kingdom.
Repentance is more than feeling horrible after sin.
You can hate the consequences of sin and still love the sin.
You can cry after pornography and return tomorrow.
You can feel guilty about emotional infidelity while continuing to protect the relationship that feeds it.
You can delete the messages while secretly hoping they message again.
Repentance eventually asks harder questions.
What needs to end?
What access needs to disappear?
What confession needs to happen?
What boundary have I been calling “legalistic” because obedience would cost me something I enjoy?
What am I protecting that is competing with Christ?
Jesus uses startling language immediately after addressing lust.
“If your right eye causes you to sin, tear it out and throw it away.”
He was not establishing self-mutilation as the cure for lust.
A person could lose an eye and still possess a lustful heart.
His language communicates the radical seriousness with which disciples must deal with sin.
In modern terms, perhaps your “right eye” is an account you need to unfollow.
An app.
A private conversation.
A friendship whose boundaries you deliberately blurred.
A phone taken into places where you repeatedly fall.
A streaming habit.
A secret password.
An emotional dependency.
A fantasy you keep revisiting because reality disappoints you.
Grace does not teach us to pet the thing Christ died to free us from.
Grace teaches us to bring it into the light.
And bringing something into the light can hurt.
There may be consequences.
Trust may need rebuilding.
Accountability may become uncomfortable.
Depending on what has happened, wise pastoral counsel or professional Christian counseling may be needed.
Forgiveness does not magically erase every earthly consequence.
But consequence is not the same thing as condemnation.
For the person who belongs to Jesus Christ, Romans 8:1 announces:
Οὐδὲν ἄρα νῦν κατάκριμα
Ouden ara nyn katakrima.
“There is therefore now no condemnation…”
For whom?
“For those who are in Christ Jesus.”
Read that carefully.
No condemnation does not mean no conviction.
Conviction says, “Come out of hiding.”
Condemnation says, “There is no point coming home.”
Conviction points toward Christ.
Condemnation tells you to run from Him.
The Gospel says run toward Him.
You may have failed again last night.
Run toward Him.
You may have spent months feeding something you knew was wrong.
Run toward Him.
You may have betrayed someone emotionally even though your bodies never touched.
Stop defending it.
Run toward Him.
You may be reading this with tears because you finally have language for something you have hidden even from yourself.
Run toward Him.
Not because your sin is small.
Because His mercy is greater.
The scandal of Christianity has always been grace.
Grace for people who do not deserve grace.
Mercy for people who cannot rewrite yesterday.
A Savior wounded for sinners who cannot save themselves.
And resurrection declaring that sin and death do not get the final word.
This is why our words at Gospel Warrior remain:
Not because Jesus pretends the scandal never happened.
He rewrites everything because He enters ruined stories with nail-scarred hands.
Peter denied Him.
Jesus restored him.
Paul persecuted His church.
Jesus transformed him into a witness of the Gospel he once tried to destroy.
The cross itself looked like history's greatest defeat until resurrection morning revealed what God was doing.
Jesus specializes in stories where everyone else thinks the final chapter has already been written.
Maybe that includes yours.
But please hear this carefully.
Jesus is not offering you permission to continue feeding lust because grace is available.
Paul confronted precisely that distortion:
“Are we to continue in sin that grace may abound? By no means!”
Romans 6:1–2.
Grace forgives.
Grace also trains.
Grace restores.
Grace also transforms.
Grace receives you covered in mud and loves you too deeply to convince you the mud is your permanent home.
So perhaps today your prayer does not need impressive vocabulary.
Maybe it sounds more like this:
Jesus, I sinned.
Not merely with what I did.
With what I wanted.
With what I watched.
With what I imagined.
With what I protected.
With what I secretly hoped would happen.
I have spent too much time defending myself instead of surrendering myself.
Forgive me.
Clean me.
Change what I love.
Teach my eyes to see people as souls, not objects.
Teach my heart to desire holiness more than secrecy.
Give me courage to close every door that keeps leading me away from You.
And when temptation whispers that I will always be this person, remind me that my identity is not written by my worst moment.
It is found in Christ.
Amen.
And now comes the difficult part.
Get up differently.
Repentance has feet.
If someone needs to be blocked, do it.
If something needs to be deleted, delete it.
If trusted Christian accountability is needed, seek it.
If you need pastoral help, ask.
If your marriage has been neglected, stop feeding imaginary intimacy while starving covenant intimacy.
If pornography has become compulsive, stop treating repeated secrecy as a private inconvenience and seek serious, trustworthy help.
And if you fall, do not transform failure into permission to remain fallen.
Confess.
Return.
Fight again.
Not to purchase God's love.
Because in Christ, grace has taught you that sin is no longer your master.
Maybe someone you love is fighting this battle silently.
Not because sharing an article earns favor with God—it does not.
Christ alone saves.
But if these words can place Scripture in front of one person who is hiding, sharing becomes an opportunity to serve.
Send this privately to the husband who is fighting for purity.
The wife carrying secret shame.
The young believer being discipled more aggressively by pornography than by Scripture.
The friend who thinks because nobody touched anybody, nothing happened.
Because temptation has an astonishing ability to make yesterday's conviction feel unreasonable tomorrow.
Come back when your heart starts negotiating again.
And please do not hide behind a polished comment section.
If this exposed something you have been defending, you do not need to describe your private sin publicly.
And if Christ has already begun restoring an area of your life you once believed could never change, tell someone beneath this article.
Your testimony may become somebody else's reason to stop hiding.
Do it as support for Gospel work, not as payment to God.
No purchase can earn blessing, forgiveness, salvation, or spiritual status.
Those belong to the realm of grace, and salvation is God's gift in Christ.

But financial support can help Gospel-centered work continue reaching people, producing biblical resources, and placing Christ-centered truth before more eyes. Giving and supporting Christian ministry can therefore become one practical expression of stewardship and partnership in Gospel work when it is done freely, wisely, cheerfully, and for God's glory—not under spiritual coercion.
Not because clicking “Share” makes you righteous.
Jesus does that which you could never do for yourself.
Share because somewhere behind another perfectly normal profile may be a person whispering:
“I never touched them. Surely this doesn't count.”
And perhaps God will use the truth of His Word appearing on their screen to interrupt a secret compromise before it becomes a public catastrophe.
One more thing.
You never touched them.
Maybe nobody ever discovered it.
Maybe nobody ever will.
But Jesus saw the heart.
And remarkably, He did not turn His face away.
He is calling you out of darkness because He intends something better than helping you become more talented at hiding.
He wants your heart.
Not the edited version.
Not the Sunday version.
Not the version your spouse sees.
Not the version your followers see.
The real one.
The wandering one.
The wounded one.
The lustful one.
The lonely one.
The ashamed one.
Bring that heart to Jesus.
Repent.
Believe the Gospel.
Receive mercy.
Then let the Spirit teach that same heart how to love what is holy.
Because one day you may discover that the most beautiful part of your story was not that nobody ever found out what happened inside you.
It was that Jesus already knew—and instead of leaving you there, He called you home.
The heart you were terrified Jesus would expose may become the very place where you remember how deeply you needed His cross.
